title: Object storage-backed databases: S3-native and tiered storage
summary: How databases and logs keep durable data in S3: batching writes into few large objects, committing through metadata with CAS fencing, caching reads, and when tiered storage beats S3-native.
outcomes: Explain why per-request pricing and 100 ms latency force object storage-backed systems to batch writes into few large objects
Compute the monthly PUT bill and average ack latency for a given flush interval and number of writers
Explain how data-then-metadata commits and conditional writes fence zombie writers
Estimate read latency from cache hit rate and explain how Neon keeps S3 off the commit and query path
Choose between tiered storage, S3-native and quorum-log hybrids from latency, cost and retention needs

lessons.title: Object storage is a strange kind of disk

blocks.md: A classic database or Kafka broker keeps its data on the local disks of the machine that serves it, and replicates that data to other machines for safety. The data and the server are welded together. When a broker dies, a replacement must copy everything the dead one held, and the KIP-405 authors note that recovery and rebalancing time is proportional to the amount of data stored locally on the broker.

**Object storage-backed databases** cut that weld. The durable copy of the data lives in an object store such as Amazon S3, and the servers become mostly **stateless compute**: they hold caches and in-flight buffers, but losing one loses nothing that was acknowledged. Any node can serve any request, so scaling out means starting a process, not moving terabytes.

blocks.title: From stateful brokers to stateless compute over S3

scenes.caption: Shared-nothing: each node owns the data on its own disk and replicates it to peers over the network. Data and server are tied together.
Node C fails. Its replacement must re-copy everything Disk C held from the surviving replicas before it is fully useful. The bigger the disk, the longer this takes.
Object storage-backed: the durable copy lives in S3, and a small metadata store records which objects make up the database. Nodes keep only caches.
Now losing Node C loses only a cache. A fresh node starts, reads the metadata, and can serve any request at once. Scaling out moves no data.

blocks.md:
What S3 gives you, per the AWS docs:

- **Durability and availability**: S3 Standard is designed for 99.999999999% durability and 99.99% availability, with data stored in at least 3 Availability Zones.
- **Strong read-after-write consistency**: after a successful PUT or DELETE, any later GET or LIST sees it. Updates to a single key are atomic: a reader gets the old object or the new one, never a mix.
- **Low storage price**: USD 0.023 per GB-month for S3 Standard in us-east-1 (first 50 TB).

What it does not give you:

- **No append or in-place update** in S3 Standard (general purpose buckets). A PUT writes a whole object. Changing one byte means writing a new object. Only the S3 Express One Zone class allows appending to an object.
- **No atomic multi-key update.** The docs say updates are key-based, and two concurrent PUTs to one key resolve by last writer wins.
- **Every request costs money and time.** In us-east-1 a PUT costs USD 0.005 per 1,000 and a GET USD 0.0004 per 1,000. AWS cites roughly 100 to 200 ms for small objects, and at least 3,500 writes or 5,500 reads per second per prefix before scaling kicks in.

blocks.prompt: A B-tree engine writes dirty 4 KiB pages. Suppose you map each page to its own S3 object and write 1 GiB of data that way. Compare the PUT bill to the cost of simply storing that 1 GiB for a month.
blocks.reveal: 1 GiB is 262,144 pages, so 262,144 PUTs at USD 0.005 per 1,000 costs about **USD 1.31**. Storing 1 GiB for a month costs USD 0.023. Writing it once in 4 KiB pieces costs about **57 months of storage**, and each PUT also takes on the order of 100 ms. Written as sixteen 64 MiB objects it costs USD 0.00008.

blocks.title: Writing 1 GiB to S3: object size decides the bill

scenes.caption: Baseline: one GiB in S3 Standard for one month costs USD 0.023.
Writing it as 16 objects of 64 MiB is 16 PUTs: USD 0.00008, too small to see. Large objects make request cost negligible.
Writing it as 262,144 objects of 4 KiB costs USD 1.31, about 57 times the monthly storage price. Per-request pricing punishes small writes.

blocks.md: S3 is not just a slow disk. A disk charges nothing per write and lets you overwrite 4 KiB in place. S3 charges per request, writes whole immutable objects, and takes tens to a couple of hundred milliseconds per request. Every design in this course reshapes writes into **few, large, immutable objects**.

Real systems fall into three families, and we will study each:

1. **S3-native**: an acknowledged write is already in object storage. WarpStream (Kafka protocol), SlateDB (an LSM key-value store) and turbopuffer (vector and full-text search) work this way.
2. **Fast log plus object storage**: commits go to a small replicated log and pages reach S3 later. Neon's Postgres storage works this way.
3. **Tiered storage**: local disks stay primary, and old data moves to S3. Kafka's KIP-405 works this way.

Object storage is cheap, durable and shared, which makes compute stateless. The price is high per-request latency and a per-request fee. Everything else follows from batching writes and caching reads to pay that price rarely.

blocks.question: Which S3 guarantee is what lets a brand-new node read a file that another node wrote a moment ago, without any coordination between the two nodes?
options: Eleven nines of durability
Strong read-after-write consistency for PUTs
Storage across at least 3 Availability Zones
Per-prefix request rate scaling
blocks.explain: Durability and multiple AZs keep data safe, but a reader could still see a stale or missing object if S3 were eventually consistent. Strong read-after-write consistency means any GET or LIST that starts after a successful PUT returns the new object, so a fresh node can trust what it reads.

blocks.question: A team builds a Kafka-like log by writing every produced record as its own S3 object. Traffic is 20,000 small records per second into one prefix. What breaks first?
options: Durability, because small objects are stored in one AZ
Nothing, S3 scales automatically and instantly
Request rate and cost: 20,000 PUTs per second is far above the 3,500 per prefix guideline and costs about USD 259,200 a month
Consistency, because LIST will miss new objects
blocks.explain: 20,000 PUT/s x 2,592,000 s per month x USD 0.000005 = USD 259,200 a month. S3 guides at least 3,500 writes per second per prefix and returns 503 Slow Down while scaling. Durability and LIST consistency are not the problem.

lessons.title: Batching writes: the cost versus latency dial

blocks.md: Recall **group commit** from the WAL course: many transactions share one fsync, so the cost of the slow operation is split across them. Object storage-backed systems apply the same idea to PUTs. A writer buffers incoming requests for a **flush interval** $T$, then writes everything as one object. Every request in the batch waits for that PUT before it is acknowledged.

blocks.caption: W is the number of independent object streams (writers, or partitions if each gets its own file). At USD 0.005 per 1,000 PUTs, one PUT per second costs USD 12.96 a month.

blocks.md: WarpStream's architecture docs give the naive case: one file per Kafka partition every 100 ms gives Kafka-like latency, but costs roughly USD 130 per partition per month in PUTs alone. Check it: 10 PUT/s x 2,592,000 s x USD 0.000005 = **USD 129.60**. One file every 30 seconds costs only USD 0.432, but 30 seconds of latency is not acceptable for a streaming system.

blocks.title: Monthly PUT bill versus flush interval

scenes.caption: One partition, one file per flush. At T = 100 ms the bill is USD 129.60 a month, matching the WarpStream docs. Cost falls as 1/T: ten times longer buffering, ten times cheaper.
Now 1,000 partitions, each with its own file. At T = 250 ms that is 4,000 PUT/s and USD 51,840 a month, above the 3,500 PUT/s per prefix guideline too.
Pack all partitions into one file per agent. Three agents at T = 250 ms make 12 PUT/s: USD 155.52 a month. Cost now scales with agents, not partitions.
Drag A or P. The gap between the curves is the factor P/A, here more than 300 times, at the same latency.

blocks.md: That is WarpStream's design. Its stateless **Agents** buffer Produce requests from many clients and partitions, and by default flush after **250 ms or 8 MiB, whichever comes first**. Each file holds records from many topic-partitions. Only after the file is in object storage *and* its metadata is committed does the Agent acknowledge the batch. Compaction in the background later merges these mixed files so that each partition's data sits together for efficient replay, much like LSM compaction merges small sorted runs.

scenes.caption: Three producers send records at 10, 120 and 240 ms. The Agent holds them in one in-memory buffer. Simplified model: PUT takes 150 ms (mid-range of AWS's 100 to 200 ms), metadata commit 10 ms.
At 250 ms the time trigger fires. The whole buffer becomes one object and is PUT to S3. A new buffer starts collecting the next batch.
The PUT succeeds at 400 ms; the Agent commits the file's metadata, done at 410 ms, then acks all three. Latencies: r1 400 ms, r2 290 ms, r3 170 ms.

blocks.caption: With requests arriving uniformly, the average wait in the buffer is T/2. Numbers are this lesson's simplified model, not a benchmark.

blocks.prompt: Ingest grows to 64 MiB/s on one Agent with the default 250 ms / 8 MiB limits. How often does it flush now, and what happens to the average buffer wait?
blocks.reveal: 8 MiB fills in 8 / 64 = 0.125 s, so the **size trigger** fires first: the Agent flushes every 125 ms, 8 PUT/s, each object 8 MiB. The average buffer wait halves to about 62.5 ms. Below 32 MiB/s (8 MiB per 250 ms) the time trigger wins and objects are smaller. Busy writers get both lower latency and a fixed number of bytes per PUT.

blocks.md: The time limit bounds latency for a quiet writer. The size limit bounds memory and object size for a busy one. Tuning both is the main knob of every S3-native write path.

blocks.question: In the model above (T = 250 ms, PUT 150 ms, commit 10 ms) average latency is 285 ms. You halve T to 125 ms. What happens?
options: Latency falls to about 222.5 ms and PUT cost doubles
Latency halves to about 142 ms and PUT cost is unchanged
Latency is unchanged because the PUT dominates
Latency falls to about 222.5 ms and PUT cost halves
blocks.explain: Only the buffer wait T/2 shrinks, from 125 to 62.5 ms, so the average becomes 222.5 ms; the PUT and commit times do not change. Flushing twice as often makes twice as many PUTs, so the request bill doubles. That is the dial: you trade money for latency, and the PUT time is a floor you cannot buffer away.

blocks.question: To cut latency further, an engineer changes the Agent to acknowledge a Produce request as soon as it lands in the in-memory buffer. What does this break?
options: Ordering within a partition
Nothing, since S3 is durable
Compaction, because files get smaller
Durability: if the Agent crashes before the PUT, acknowledged records are lost
blocks.explain: The buffer is memory in a stateless process. WarpStream never acknowledges a write until it is in object storage and committed to the metadata store, which is what lets it lose every Agent without losing acknowledged data. Acking from memory turns a crash into data loss.

lessons.title: Committing to object storage: metadata, CAS and fencing

blocks.md: A database is many objects, but S3 is atomic only per key. So every design keeps a small **source of truth** that says which objects make up the database right now. WarpStream uses a separate metadata store (each Virtual Cluster is a replicated state machine that journals every operation to a strongly consistent log). SlateDB, an LSM tree that writes everything to object storage, keeps a **manifest** object in the bucket, much like RocksDB's MANIFEST file.

The write protocol is then always two steps:

1. **PUT the data** under a fresh, unique object name. Nobody references it yet, so nobody can see it.
2. **Commit** by atomically adding a reference to it in the metadata. Only now acknowledge the client.

In WarpStream the commit step is also where ordering is decided: files may reach S3 out of order, but the metadata store assigns offsets when it commits each batch, so any Agent can write any partition and Kafka ordering still holds.

blocks.title: The two-step write: data first, then metadata

scenes.caption: The producer sends records for partition 7. The Agent batches them with other partitions' records into one file.
Step 1: the file is written under a unique name. It is durable now, but no metadata points to it, so no reader can see it.
Step 2: the commit records which offset ranges of which partitions live in file-42. The metadata store assigns the offsets, which fixes the order.
Only after both steps does the producer get its ack. Acknowledged means durable in S3 and visible through the metadata.

blocks.prompt: The Agent crashes right after S3 returns 200 OK for file-42, before the metadata commit. Is any acknowledged data lost? Can consumers see file-42?
blocks.reveal: No acknowledged data is lost, because the producer never received an ack; it will retry through another Agent. Consumers never see file-42 either, because readers find data only through the metadata. File-42 is an **orphan**: durable but unreferenced garbage that a background cleaner can delete. Writing data first and committing second makes crashes leave garbage, never corruption.

blocks.md: The harder problem is a **zombie writer**. Single-writer designs such as SlateDB assume exactly one process writes the database. Suppose writer A stalls in a long GC pause, an orchestrator decides it is dead, and starts writer B. Then A wakes up and, unaware, keeps writing. Without protection both write WAL files and the manifest, and S3's default rule for concurrent PUTs to one key is last writer wins.

The fix needs an atomic **create if absent**. S3 added conditional writes in August 2024: with the header `If-None-Match: *`, a PUT succeeds only if no object has that key. If several conditional writes race for the same key, the first to finish wins and the rest get `412 Precondition Failed`. With `If-Match: <ETag>`, a PUT succeeds only if the object is unchanged, which gives compare-and-swap (CAS) on a mutable object.

blocks.code:
aws s3api put-object --bucket my-db --key wal/00000000000000000002.sst \
    --body fence.sst --if-none-match "*"
# 200 OK                    -> we own slot 2
# 412 Precondition Failed   -> someone else wrote slot 2 first
blocks.caption: Conditional create with the AWS CLI, as in the S3 docs. The key is a WAL slot named by a zero-padded 20-digit ID, as SlateDB names its WAL files.

blocks.md:
SlateDB's manifest design (RFC-0001) builds **fencing** on top of that. The manifest holds a `writer_epoch`, and every WAL SST is stamped with the epoch of the writer that wrote it.

1. On startup a writer reads the latest manifest, increments `writer_epoch`, and writes the next numbered manifest with CAS.
2. It then writes an empty **fencing SST** with its new epoch at the next WAL ID, again with CAS.
3. If that CAS fails, it reads the winner's epoch. Older epoch: move to the next ID and retry. Newer epoch: it has been fenced and must halt.

blocks.title: Fencing a zombie writer in the WAL (RFC-0001 example)

scenes.caption: Writer A runs with epoch 1 and writes WAL SSTs 0 and 1. Each SST records the writer epoch e1.
Writer B starts, bumps the manifest epoch to 2, then writes an empty fencing SST at slot 2 with If-None-Match. It wins. Writer A is now fenced, but does not know it yet.
Zombie A wakes and tries to write its next SST at slot 2. The conditional PUT returns 412. A reads slot 2, sees epoch 2 is newer than its own, and halts.
Writer B continues at slot 3. WAL IDs stay contiguous and every slot was written exactly once, so readers replaying the WAL never see two histories.

blocks.md: Leases and timeouts alone do not fence. A paused process cannot notice that its lease expired while it was paused, so its next write happens anyway. Safety comes from the **storage rejecting** the stale writer: a conditional PUT on a slot the new writer already claimed.
Write data under fresh names, then commit a reference atomically. Use a create-if-absent or compare-and-swap on the commit point so that exactly one writer can ever extend the history.

blocks.question: New writer B (epoch 2) tries its fencing write at WAL slot 2 and gets 412. Reading slot 2, it finds an SST from old writer A with epoch 1. What should B do?
options: Halt, because it lost the race
Overwrite slot 2 without a condition, since its epoch is higher
Retry the fencing write at slot 3
Wait for A's lease to expire, then retry slot 2
blocks.explain: This is RFC-0001's second example. A simply got one more SST in before B's fence. Because the winner's epoch is older, B moves to the next ID and retries; once its fence lands, A will hit B's SST and halt. Halting is only right when the winner's epoch is newer. Overwriting would destroy A's acknowledged data.

blocks.question: Why does SlateDB write each manifest version as a new numbered object (00...02.manifest, 00...03.manifest) instead of overwriting one manifest key?
options: S3 cannot overwrite objects
With create-if-absent on the next number, two writers cannot both install version N+1; a plain overwrite of one key is last writer wins
Numbered objects are cheaper to PUT
LIST is only consistent for new keys
blocks.explain: S3 can overwrite, and LIST is strongly consistent, but concurrent unconditional PUTs to one key resolve as last writer wins, silently losing an update. A conditional create on the next ID means exactly one of two racing writers succeeds, which is a compare-and-swap on the database state.

lessons.title: Keeping object storage off the hot read path

blocks.md: Writes can hide S3 latency behind batching, but a read must answer one specific question now. If every read paid 100 to 200 ms, nobody would use these systems. So every design puts a **cache hierarchy** in front of S3: memory, then local NVMe SSD, then sometimes a caching tier of other nodes, and only on a full miss, object storage. The question is how good the hit rate must be.

blocks.caption: h is the cache hit rate. Simplified model for this lesson: a hit costs 1 ms and a miss (one S3 GET) costs 150 ms.

blocks.title: Expected read latency versus cache hit rate

scenes.caption: With a 1 ms hit and a 150 ms miss, a 90% hit rate gives 15.9 ms on average. Misses are 10% of reads but contribute 15 of those ms.
At 99% the average is 2.49 ms. Going from 90% to 99% cuts latency more than 6 times: the curve is steepest near h = 1.
Raise the miss latency to 300 ms (a slow tail GET). The whole line steepens; only a very high hit rate keeps the average low.

blocks.md: LSM trees make this worse. A point lookup may check every sorted run that could hold the key. With 5 runs and the key in the last one, five sequential GETs cost 750 ms in our model. **Bloom filters**, kept in the cache, let the reader skip runs that surely lack the key. At a 1% false-positive rate the expected number of GETs is $1 + 4 \times 0.01 = 1.04$, about 156 ms. Readers also fetch only the needed blocks with byte-range GETs, which the S3 docs recommend for large objects.

blocks.title: One LSM point lookup on S3, 5 sorted runs (model)

scenes.caption: Without filters, a key in the oldest run costs a GET per run: 5 x 150 = 750 ms.
Cached Bloom filters rule out runs without the key, so on average 1.04 GETs: 156 ms.
If the data block is also cached, the lookup never touches S3: about 1 ms in this model. Cache filters and index blocks first; they are small and every read needs them.

blocks.md: **Neon** (now also branded Lakebase Postgres) shows the most complete version. Postgres runs unchanged on a compute node, but instead of flushing WAL to a local disk it streams WAL to several **safekeepers**. A transaction commits once a majority of safekeepers have stored the record, using a Paxos-based protocol. A **pageserver** consumes the WAL, materializes page versions and uploads them to object storage asynchronously. Compute reads RAM, then its local NVMe cache, then asks the pageserver for a page at a given LSN (log sequence number). Compute never reads object storage directly.

blocks.title: Neon: object storage behind the pageserver, never in front of a query

scenes.caption: Commit: compute streams WAL to three safekeepers. Two acks make a majority, so the transaction commits even though safekeeper 3 is slow. No S3 request is on this path.
In the background the pageserver ingests WAL, builds page versions and uploads them to object storage. This is asynchronous: commits never wait for it.
Read, cache hit: the page is in RAM or on local NVMe. Memory or microsecond-level latency, no network round trip.
Read, cache miss: compute asks the pageserver for the page at an LSN. If needed the pageserver loads a base image from object storage and replays WAL. Only the pageserver ever pays S3 latency.

blocks.md: Route repeat reads to the node whose cache already holds the data. WarpStream assigns file ranges to Agents with consistent hashing inside each Availability Zone, so each chunk is fetched from S3 about once per zone. turbopuffer routes a namespace's queries to the same node; its docs report a cold first query at p50 874 ms and cached queries at p50 14 ms (1M documents), and suggest a pre-flight query to warm the cache.

blocks.question: In Neon, why does a COMMIT not include the latency of an object storage PUT?
options: Postgres batches commits for up to a second
Durability comes from a majority of safekeepers storing the WAL; pages reach object storage later, off the commit path
The compute node's local NVMe is replicated
Object storage writes are done with S3 Express One Zone
blocks.explain: Neon defines commit as WAL acknowledged by a quorum of safekeepers. The pageserver materializes pages and uploads them to object storage asynchronously. If a safekeeper dies, the quorum continues; if the pageserver dies, its state is rebuilt from WAL and object storage.

blocks.question: A service runs at a 99% cache hit rate. During a deploy, all nodes restart with empty caches. What do users see, and what is the best mitigation?
options: Nothing, S3 is fast enough
Writes fail until caches refill
A latency spike toward S3 GET latency until caches warm; pre-warm hot data and roll restarts so routing keeps most caches warm
Stale reads, because caches were cleared
blocks.explain: With h near 0 every read is a miss, so latency jumps from about 2.5 ms toward 150 ms in our model. Data is never stale or lost, since S3 holds it. Rolling restarts and pre-warming the hottest objects keep the hit rate high while nodes come back.

lessons.title: Tiered storage versus S3-native: choosing a design

blocks.md: **Tiered storage** is the conservative design. Kafka's KIP-405 keeps brokers, local disks and replication exactly as before, and adds a second, remote tier such as S3 or HDFS. Most Kafka reads are **tail reads** of fresh data served from the OS page cache; older data is read rarely, for backfill or recovery. So recent segments stay local and completed segments move to the remote tier.

The mechanism, per KIP-405 and the [Kafka topic configs](https://kafka.apache.org/41/generated/topic_config.html):

- A topic opts in with `remote.storage.enable=true` (brokers need `remote.log.storage.system.enable=true`).
- The partition leader copies **rolled** segments (never the active one) with their indexes to remote storage through a pluggable `RemoteStorageManager`. Segment metadata goes through `RemoteLogMetadataManager`, by default the internal topic `__remote_log_metadata`.
- Two retention limits: `retention.ms` for the whole log (default 7 days) and `local.retention.ms` for local disks (default -2, meaning the same as `retention.ms`).
- A local segment is not deleted until its copy to remote storage has succeeded.
- A fetch for an offset no longer local is served from the remote tier.

blocks.title: Segments moving from broker disk to the remote tier

scenes.caption: Six segments on the leader's disk. s5 is active (being appended). s0 to s4 are rolled. Nothing is remote yet.
The leader copies rolled segments s0 to s4 to the remote tier with their indexes. The active segment s5 is never copied until it rolls.
Local retention expires for s0 to s2, which are safely remote, so they are deleted locally. Disk now holds only recent data; tail reads still hit the page cache.
A backfill consumer asks for an offset in s1. It is not local, so the broker reads it from the remote tier. Slower, but the same Kafka API and the same topic.

blocks.md:
**Worked example.** One partition ingests 5 MiB/s with `retention.ms` of 7 days and replication factor 3.

- Without tiering each replica holds 5 x 604,800 / 1,024 = **2,953.1 GiB**, so 8,859.4 GiB across three brokers.
- With `local.retention.ms` at 6 hours each replica holds 5 x 21,600 / 1,024 = **105.5 GiB** plus the active segment, 28 times less.
- The remote tier stores one logical copy, which S3 Standard spreads over at least 3 AZs itself: 2,953.1 GiB x USD 0.023 = about USD 67.92 a month.
- At the default `segment.bytes` of 1 GiB, a segment rolls every 1,024 / 5 = 204.8 s.

blocks.title: Local disk per replica for one 5 MiB/s partition

scenes.caption: No tiering: every replica keeps all 7 days, 2,953.1 GiB. Replacing a broker means re-copying this much per partition.
Tiered: 105.5 GiB per replica plus the active segment. Broker replacement and rebalancing copy 28 times less data.

blocks.md: **S3-native** goes further. WarpStream's docs stress that it is *not* tiered storage: Agents have no local disks, there is no broker-to-broker replication, and a write is acknowledged once it is in S3 and committed to metadata. That removes cross-AZ replication traffic, which WarpStream estimates at an effective USD 0.05 per GB at AWS retail prices, and makes Agents fully stateless. The cost is produce latency of hundreds of milliseconds instead of a few, because every acknowledged byte waits for a PUT.

How to choose:

- **Write latency budget.** Need single-digit milliseconds? Keep a fast replicated log on the commit path (Kafka with tiering, or Neon's safekeepers). Hundreds of milliseconds fine? S3-native is simplest.
- **Where durability comes from.** Tiered and Neon: your own replicated disks first, S3 later. S3-native: S3 alone.
- **What must scale.** Long retention with small hot data favours tiering. Elastic, bursty compute favours stateless nodes over S3.
- **Read pattern.** Tail reads are served from memory in any design; backfills and cold queries pay S3 latency in all of them.

Tiered storage moves *old* data to S3 and leaves the write path alone. S3-native moves the *write path itself* to S3, trading commit latency for stateless compute. Hybrids like Neon put a small quorum log in front so commits stay fast while object storage holds the bulk.

blocks.question: A topic has segment.bytes = 1 GiB, ingest of 5 MiB/s, tiered storage on, and local.retention.ms set to 1 minute. How much data can still be on the leader's local disk?
options: About 300 MiB, one minute of data
Zero, everything goes to S3 within a minute
At least the active segment, up to 1 GiB, because only rolled segments are copied and deleted
The full 7 days, because local retention is ignored
blocks.explain: Only rolled segments are copied to the remote tier, and local segments are not deleted until their copy succeeds. The active segment rolls only after 1 GiB (about 205 s at 5 MiB/s), so it always stays local. Retention works per segment, not per byte.

blocks.question: Which workload is the best fit for S3-native (diskless) rather than tiered Kafka?
options: Log and telemetry pipelines with high throughput, bursty load, and an end-to-end latency budget of about a second
Payment authorization needing 5 ms produce latency
A small cluster with 1 hour of retention and steady load
A compacted topic used as a key-value changelog with sub-millisecond reads
blocks.explain: S3-native systems acknowledge after a PUT and a metadata commit, so produce latency is hundreds of milliseconds, fine for telemetry but not a 5 ms payment path. Their payoff, stateless scaling and no cross-AZ replication, matters most for large, bursty, high-throughput streams. A small steady cluster gains little.

blocks.question: A team enables tiered storage and expects produce latency to drop because brokers now have less data on disk. What actually happens to produce latency?
options: It drops, since disks are less full
It rises to S3 PUT latency
It becomes unpredictable because acks wait for remote copies
It is essentially unchanged: produce still goes through the leader and in-sync replicas; remote copying happens later, for rolled segments only
blocks.explain: Tiering changes what happens to data after a segment rolls. The produce path, leader append plus replication to in-sync replicas, is the same as without tiering, so latency does not drop or rise because of it. The wins are smaller disks and faster broker replacement and rebalancing.
